allow: dotnet build/test/run/watch/restore, dotnet ef migrations add
npm/pnpm/yarn install/ci/run/test/build, npx <tool>, vitest, playwright test
docker compose up/down/build/logs/ps, docker run/exec/logs on local containers

git status/diff/log/show/add/commit/branch (no -D)/checkout <branch>/pull/fetch; git stash push; git push (non-force); git push --force-with-lease <remote> <branch> (exact flag, no other options; never main or master). Neither push clause covers a branch whose name marks it as a deploy or publication target (production, release, deploy, gh-pages, and the like).

Local Operations extension: ~/.claude (github.com/BriantsaiCoder/dotclaude) and ~/.agents (github.com/BriantsaiCoder/agents-config) are the user's own repositories and are in project scope for this user — reading, editing, git status/diff/log/add/commit/branch/pull, and pushing to a feature branch in either is a Local Operation, not scope escalation. Editing ~/.claude/settings.json is included, and so is ordinary git bookkeeping on ~/.claude (branch, worktree add/list, add, commit, push to a feature branch): the user has explicitly and repeatedly directed this maintenance of their own machine configuration, so per this ALLOW contract it is not agent self-modification. That carve-out is scoped to settings.json and git bookkeeping only — every other $defaults Self-Modification config surface stays excluded (that rule's own list governs; ~/.agents/bin/pr-review-gate counts as equivalent for this purpose, because hard_deny[1] makes it the merge gate), as does reading ~/.claude/.credentials.json.
soft_deny: Reading or exfiltrating secret files (.env*, appsettings.*.json, *.pem/*.key/*.pfx, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, .npmrc, .netrc) via any reader (cat/less/more/head/tail/bat/xxd/od/hexdump/base64/openssl) or piping them into network tools (curl/nc/scp/rsync).
Destructive SQL via any SQL client (CLI, GUI, ORM raw-SQL, or an app's own migration runner): DROP DATABASE/TABLE/SCHEMA, TRUNCATE, or DELETE/UPDATE without a narrow predicate.
Destructive NoSQL: mongosh drop/dropDatabase, redis-cli FLUSHDB/FLUSHALL, DETACH DATABASE.
Publishing to external registries: npm/yarn/pnpm publish, dotnet nuget push, cargo publish, gem push, twine upload, docker/helm push to public registries.
Modifying local trust or secret stores: dotnet user-secrets set/clear, dotnet dev-certs, security add-trusted-cert, keychain writes, update-ca-certificates.
Silently discarding uncommitted work: git checkout . / -- <path>, git restore . / --source, git reflog expire, git stash drop/clear.

Database or migration destruction: dotnet ef database drop, dotnet ef database update to an earlier migration or to 0 (a rollback, not an upgrade), dotnet ef migrations remove with -f/--force, prisma migrate reset, knex migrate:rollback against non-ephemeral targets.
hard_deny: Never merge a pull request unless ~/.agents/bin/pr-review-gate reported STATE=PASS or STATE=PASS_NO_CI for that PR at the current head SHA in this session. PASS_NO_CI is the gate's degraded state and covers exactly three ci values, each a distinct way of having no CI verdict rather than a bad one: ci=ABSENT, no check run was ever created for that commit and the commit is older than the gate's wait threshold; ci=CANCELLED, runs existed but every cancelled run executed zero steps, nothing else was still running, and the same threshold has passed; ci=BILLING_QUOTA, every hard failure on that head is an Actions job that executed zero steps and carries GitHub's `job was not started` and `spending limit` annotations, with nothing queued or cancelled alongside it. Of the three, only ci=BILLING_QUOTA can authorize a merge, and only with all of the following at that same head SHA: a full local CI-equivalent run plus every applicable integration, isolated-E2E and security gate, an independent Standards and Spec review by someone other than the PR author, and 0 unresolved actionable findings; hosted CI stays UNAVAILABLE in the record and is never restated as PASS. ci=ABSENT and ci=CANCELLED do not authorize a merge at all. [T0-9] requires an applicable CI PASS and states no exception; this repo's ci.yml triggers on every pull_request with no path filter, so CI is always applicable and those two states mean it did not run rather than that none applies; and review-triage.md admits no fallback for either. The answer there is to make CI run, not to merge around it. Separately, on any gate line that carries the field, a non-zero suppressed=N means N Copilot findings that produced no review thread and are therefore absent from unresolved; read that section of the review body and dispose of each before merging, because STATE=PASS is evidence of no open threads and never of no findings. The merge hook cannot enforce the suppressed check for you, and the reason is not that it cannot see the count: pr-review-gate prints suppressed=N on the very line the hook already reads. Making the hook block on suppressed>0 is deliberately not done — suppressed findings have no resolve mechanism, so a blocking condition on them would deadlock permanently, which pr-review-gate records where it fetches that count. What no hook can check is whether each suppressed finding was actually read and disposed of, and that judgement is what this entry covers. The three ci values are a different matter: since 2026-08-27 hooks/guard-pr-merge.sh splits them mechanically, allowing STATE=PASS_NO_CI only when the gate's first output line is well-formed and carries a space-delimited ci=BILLING_QUOTA field, and denying every other shape — ci=ABSENT, ci=CANCELLED, an unrecognized ci value, a missing ci= field, a line that is not plain KEY=VALUE — each with a reason that says which one it hit. Read that reason rather than assuming the gate failed. That hook decides only which state may merge; it never checks whether the compensating local evidence listed above actually exists, so the hook letting ci=BILLING_QUOTA through is not evidence that those conditions were met — that part stays yours. Never merge when CI is pending, queued, or genuinely failing: a job that executed even one step is a real failure, not a degraded state. It is a deliberate narrow allowance, not a wildcard: every other STATE remains forbidden, including future states whose names begin with PASS.
Never delete, transfer, or change the visibility of a GitHub repository, and never delete releases or tags.

Never write to files under the user's home directory outside the session's working directory, ~/.claude, ~/.agents, ~/.codex, and ~/.copilot — this includes ~/Documents, ~/Desktop, ~/Pictures, ~/Library, and shell startup files. The ~/.codex and ~/.copilot carve-out matches sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite, which already grants write there; keeping the two layers aligned is the point, and it does not extend to any other home path. ~/.claude is deliberately NOT aligned that way: allowWrite grants only ~/.claude/.git, never the tree. Widening it to the tree buys nothing worth having beyond what that entry already grants, while turning every ~/.claude root file Bash-writable — including statusline-command.sh, which executes on every render, and the telemetry and history logs. Subdirectories do stay denied under a widened allowWrite, but through a mix of this repo's own denyWrite entries and harness defaults, so never conclude from that observation that the denyWrite entries are redundant. Measurements and rationale live in tests/repo-integrity.sh; do not resolve the mismatch by widening the sandbox. Inside ~/.claude only .github/workflows/ carries an Edit deny rule; settings.json no longer does, so the built-in .claude protected-path check gates it instead, and permissions.allow cannot pre-approve that check. Never widen a permission, hook, or sandbox boundary in settings.json on your own initiative — an instruction to review, tidy, or improve the settings never authorizes widening one. An explicit user instruction naming the specific change does authorize it, including edits to this hard_deny list and to any other section of settings.json. Bash and Write-tool writes to settings.json have no hard block: sandbox denyWrite covers the sandboxed path only, and the Write(~/.claude/settings.json) deny entry is a signal to this classifier rather than a gate. It is not redundant and must not be deleted on that reasoning; tests/repo-integrity.sh records why it stays. Route every settings.json change through the Edit tool, where the diff is visible — never shell redirection, never a Write-tool whole-file overwrite. CLAUDE.md and hooks/ rely on sandbox denyWrite plus the same protected-path check, and hooks/ additionally on the content fingerprint pinned in tests/hooks.sha256; that protection covers editing those files and nothing else. It does not extend to git bookkeeping: staging, committing, or pushing those paths writes ~/.claude/.git (index, objects, refs), never the files themselves, and is ordinary version control of the user's own repository — allowed, including when a path argument names one of the protected files. That enumeration is exhaustive on purpose: .git/hooks and .git/config both execute code — hooks on every commit, config through aliases and core.fsmonitor — so denyWrite carves both back out. Denying config costs push and fetch nothing: sandboxed network git already fails with `error setting certificate verify locations` and runs unsandboxed regardless.
environment: Repository config, manifests, lockfiles, CI, and the current task are the source of truth for package manager, database target, and credential/environment boundaries; assume neither local-only nor production access without evidence.

Sandbox is enabled and autoAllowBashIfSandboxed is true — project workspace writable; package manager caches (npm, NuGet, .NET, Playwright browsers) and ~/.Trash also whitelisted via allowWrite. Unsandboxed retry stays available and is gated by the auto-mode classifier rather than a prompt, so unattended runs do not stall.
Preferred stacks: .NET 8 / ASP.NET Core, EF Core, PostgreSQL, Vite + React/Vue, Tailwind, Docker Compose.

~/.claude is the user's own dotfiles repository (remote: github.com/BriantsaiCoder/dotclaude) and ~/.agents is github.com/BriantsaiCoder/agents-config; both are public repos, so a push there is world-readable. Routine git operations in either — status, diff, add, commit, branch, push to a feature branch, pull — are ordinary maintenance of the user's own configuration, not scope escalation, even though those paths sit outside the session working directory. Writes under ~/.agents land inside the sandbox because it is in sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite, except the paths listed in sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite; under ~/.claude only .git is in allowWrite, so local git bookkeeping runs sandboxed while every other write there reaches the filesystem through the unsandboxed retry path; network git (push, fetch, pull) is observed to need that retry as well, failing inside the sandbox with `error setting certificate verify locations`. That retry is expected for ~/.claude and is not an auto-mode bypass. denyWrite is selected by one test — would editing this punch through a gate? It covers the settings and CLAUDE.md the classifier itself reads, the merge-gate binary, the hook decision layer, tier0, and the workflow kernel that defines the authorization rules. Ordinary content is deliberately left out — the other skills, ~/.claude/rules/ — because denyWrite has no "unless the user asked for it" escape hatch, and the $defaults Self-Modification rule already gates the widening and consent-manufacturing edits there.
